name: Question 11
problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=xy+xz+yz.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-2,-1).$
worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,-2,-1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-2,-1)+∇f(1,-2,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+2,z+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,-2,-1)=-1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =y+z\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(1,-2,-1)=-3, \\ {f}_{y} & =x+z\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(1,-2,-1)=0, \\ {f}_{z} & =x+y\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(1,-2,-1)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,-2,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,-2,-1) & =⟨-3,0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,-2,-1)+∇f(1,-2,-1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y+2,z+1⟩ \\  & =-1+⟨-3,0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y+2,z+1⟩ \\  & =-1-3(x-1)+0(y+2)-1(z+1) \\  & =1-3x-z.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Let f(x,y,z)=xy+xz+yz. Find the linear approximation of f at the point (1,−2,−1).

a
f(x,y,z)≈4−3x−z
b
f(x,y,z)≈1−3x−z
c
f(x,y,z)≈2−3x+y−z
d
f(x,y,z)≈1+3x−2z
e
f(x,y,z)≈6−3x+y−z
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The linear approximation of the function f at the point (a,b,c) is given by f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)⋅⟨x−a,y−b,z−c⟩.

So, the linear approximation of f at the point (1,−2,−1) is f(x,y,z)≈f(1,−2,−1)+∇f(1,−2,−1)⋅⟨x−1,y+2,z+1⟩.

From the definition of f, we have that f(1,−2,−1)=−1. Computing the partial derivatives, we get

fx=y+z⇒fx(1,−2,−1)=−3,fy=x+z⇒fy(1,−2,−1)=0,fz=x+y⇒fz(1,−2,−1)=−1.

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point (1,−2,−1) is given by ∇f(1,−2,−1)=⟨−3,0,−1⟩.

Finally, the linear approximation of the function f is

f(x,y,z)≈f(1,−2,−1)+∇f(1,−2,−1)⋅⟨x−1,y+2,z+1⟩=−1+⟨−3,0,−1⟩⋅⟨x−1,y+2,z+1⟩=−1−3(x−1)+0(y+2)−1(z+1)=1−3x−z.
